title: Richard Attenborough
wiki_lead:
Richard Samuel Attenborough, Baron Attenborough ( AT-ən-bər-rə; 29 August 1923 – 24 August 2014) was an English actor, film director, and producer. He won a total of two Academy Awards, four BAFTA Awards, and six Golden Globe Awards for his directing and acting career spanning seven decades. He was knighted in 1976 for services to film and in 1983 he received the BAFTA Fellowship for lifetime achievement.
As an actor, Attenborough is best remembered for his film roles in Brighton Rock (1948), I'm All Right Jack (1959), The Great Escape (1963), Seance on a Wet Afternoon (1964), The Sand Pebbles (1966), Doctor Dolittle (1967), 10 Rillington Place (1971), Jurassic Park (1993) and Miracle on 34th Street (1994). On stage, he appeared in the West End in 1952, originating the role of Detective Sergeant Trotter in Agatha Christie's murder mystery The Mousetrap, which has since become the longest-running play in London and the world.
For his directorial debut in Oh! What a Lovely War (1969), Attenborough was nominated for the BAFTA Award for Best Direction. He was additionally nominated for his films Young Winston (1972), A Bridge Too Far (1977) and Cry Freedom (1987). For the film Gandhi (1983), he received the Oscars for Best Picture and Best Director. The British Film Institute ranked Gandhi number 34 in its list of greatest British films of the 20th century. His later films include Chaplin (1992) (a biography of Charlie Chaplin), and a fifth collaboration with Anthony Hopkins in Shadowlands (1993).
Attenborough was the president of the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (RADA), of which he was an alumnus, and the British Academy of Film and Television Arts (BAFTA), as well as life president of the Premier League club Chelsea. He joined the Royal Air Force during World War II and served in the film unit, going on several bombing raids over continental Europe and filming the conflict from the rear gunner's position. He was the older brother of broadcaster and nature presenter Sir David Attenborough and motor executive John Attenborough. He was married to actress Sheila Sim from 1945 until his death.

Early life
Attenborough was born on 29 August 1923 in Cambridge, Cambridgeshire, the eldest son of three from mother Mary Attenborough (née Clegg)—a founding member of the Marriage Guidance Council—and father Frederick Levi Attenborough, a scholar and academic administrator who was a fellow at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, and wrote a standard text on Anglo-Saxon law. Attenborough was educated at Wyggeston Grammar School for Boys in Leicester and studied at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (RADA) in London.

grok_lead: Richard Samuel Attenborough, Baron Attenborough, CBE (29 August 1923 â 24 August 2014) was an English actor, director, and producer whose seven-decade career bridged stage, screen, and cultural advocacy. Born in Cambridge to an academic family, he debuted professionally on stage at age 18 and entered film acting during World War II, establishing himself with the chilling portrayal of juvenile delinquent Pinkie Brown in Brighton Rock (1947). Over subsequent decades, Attenborough built a reputation for versatile supporting roles in ensemble war films like The Great Escape (1963) and character-driven dramas such as 10 Rillington Place (1971), while also venturing into production. His directorial breakthrough came with the epic Gandhi (1982), a biographical depiction of Mohandas Gandhi's life and nonviolent resistance against British rule, which he nurtured for 20 years amid financing hurdles; the film secured eight Academy Awards, including Best Picture and Best Director for Attenborough. Subsequent efforts like Cry Freedom (1987), addressing South African apartheid, and Chaplin (1992), underscored his preference for historical narratives probing moral and political causation, though these met mixed critical and commercial reception compared to Gandhi. Knighted in 1976 and elevated to the peerage in 1993, Attenborough wielded influence in British arts institutions, serving as president of the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art and championing film preservation, while enduring personal tragedy including the 2004 tsunami deaths of his daughter and grandchildren.
